Peru Imposes Temporary Tariff on Imported Gas Equipment, Utilities Brace for Impact

LIMA—The Peruvian government has imposed a 25% tariff on imported gas metering and distribution equipment, a move officials say is designed to support domestic manufacturers and enhance national energy security. The policy, enacted last week and slated to last at least six months, is already reshaping the operating landscape for the country’s Gas & Water Utilities industry.

Under the new measure, all imported gas meters, pressure regulators, and related infrastructure components now face the additional levy at customs. The Ministry of Economy and Finance stated that the tariff aims to “promote local capacity and reduce external dependencies” amid growing demand for urban gas distribution.

Gas utility firms have responded by warning of increased costs and potential project delays. “We are reassessing procurement for ongoing network expansions in Arequipa and Trujillo,” said María Torres, director of regulatory affairs at Suministros Andinos, one of Peru’s largest urban gas distributors. “Our reliance on specialized imported meters means this tariff will increase our costs by up to 18% on current projects. In the short term, this may slow rollout timelines and affect staffing requirements.”

Industry association Cámara de Servicios Públicos (CSP) estimates that more than 65% of advanced metering devices used by Peruvian utilities are sourced from overseas suppliers, primarily in Europe and East Asia. “Domestic alternatives are not yet available in sufficient quantity or quality,” CSP president Felipe Ramos noted. “Utilities may be forced to postpone upgrades or repairs until the supply situation stabilizes.”

The tariff has prompted some gas utilities to put capital investments on hold. At least two major infrastructure projects, including a planned gas distribution expansion in the southern region, have been delayed pending reassessment of budgets. Executives from Agua y Gas del Sur cited “significant uncertainty” about equipment costs and delivery schedules.

Workers in the sector are also feeling the effects, with several utilities announcing temporary reductions in overtime and non-essential maintenance. “Until we have clarity on equipment availability and pricing, we are prioritizing only critical repairs,” said a union representative at Red de Gas Metropolitana, which operates over 2,000 kilometers of pipeline in Lima.

Government officials have said the tariff will be reviewed after six months, with consultations expected between industry leaders and the Ministry of Energy and Mines. In the meantime, utility firms and their workers are closely monitoring the evolving situation, as the Gas & Water Utilities industry adjusts to the new policy environment.
